# R3: Inference and model comparison {.unnumbered}

::: {.week-meta}
Core reading
: @field2024, the linear model (regression) chapter: the sections on hierarchical regression and comparing models (about 60 minutes)

Data
: [Student Life Survey](../course/dataset.qmd), clean file: `wellbeing`, `work_hours`, `commute`, `support`, `efficacy`

App
: Nested regression models

Task style
: Worked example: reproduce, then change one thing and predict the result

:::

## By the end of this week you can

- Interpret standard errors, confidence intervals and t tests for coefficients.
- Say when one model is nested in another.
- Run and interpret the F test for the change in R².
- Draw two nested models and mark the paths fixed at zero.

## Warm-up

Answer from memory at the start of the session. It takes two minutes and makes earlier ideas easier to recall later.

1. What is a partial regression coefficient?
2. In a simple regression, how is the slope related to the covariance? (R1)

<details class="answers">
<summary>Check your answers</summary>

1. The expected change in the outcome for a one-unit change in that predictor, holding the other predictors constant.
2. b = cov(X, Y) / var(X): the covariance scaled by the variance of the predictor.

</details>

## This week in brief

Standard errors, t tests and confidence intervals tell you how precisely each coefficient is estimated. Comparing a simpler model with a fuller one tests whether a whole set of extra predictors adds anything. When the simpler model is the fuller model with some paths fixed at zero, the two are *nested*, and the F test for the change in R² compares them. Comparing nested models comes back repeatedly later in the course.

## In the session

- Nested models: what makes one model a special case of another, using the path diagrams.
- The F test for the change in R², with the app: what it tests, and how sample size and overlap between predictors affect it.

## After the session

Read the core reading on hierarchical (blockwise) regression and the F test for the change in R².

## Your task this week

1. **Predict first:** how much of the variance in wellbeing will paid work and commute time explain on their own?
2. Run a hierarchical regression of `wellbeing`: block 1 `work_hours` and `commute`; block 2 add `support` and `efficacy`. Request "R squared change".
3. Interpret R² for each block, ΔR² and the F test for the change. Does the coefficient for `work_hours` change between blocks?
4. Draw both models as path diagrams and mark the paths that Model 1 fixes at zero.

## For your SEM log

Write your answers in your log first; then compare.

1. What makes two regression models nested? Draw an example.
2. With ΔR² unchanged, why does a larger N make the F test significant?
3. Why might the coefficient for work_hours change when support and efficacy are added?

<details class="answers model">
<summary>Compare with model answers (after writing your own)</summary>

1. Model A is nested in Model B if A can be obtained from B by fixing some of B's parameters (here, setting paths to zero). Model 1 (work, commute → wellbeing) is nested in Model 2 (work, commute, support, efficacy → wellbeing).
2. F compares the change in R² with the unexplained variance per residual degree of freedom. More cases give more residual degrees of freedom, so the same ΔR² is estimated more precisely and F grows.
3. If work hours correlate with support or efficacy, part of their association with wellbeing in Model 1 was carried by those variables. Here the correlations are small, so the change is small too.

</details>
